# Exercise 3.3 — The best fit line {#sec-best-fit}


## Overview

The last exercise scored lines that were handed to you. This one turns that
round: the loss becomes a function of the intercept and the slope, and fitting
becomes a search for the pair that scores lowest. You will score candidate
lines by hand, then score fifteen thousand of them at once and look at the
surface they trace out — which is the thing every fitting procedure is trying
to find the bottom of.


:::::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

### Where we left off

Exercise 3.2 scored lines that somebody else had drawn. Load the same 80
patients, fit the line `lm()` chooses, and rebuild the contaminated copy — the
one with patients 1, 3 and 5 tripled — because the last task needs both.

```{r}
library(tidyverse)

glu <- read_csv("data/glucose_study.csv")

fit_ols <- lm(glucose ~ age, data = glu)

glu_bad <- glu |>
  mutate(glucose = if_else(row_number() %in% c(1, 3, 5),
                           glucose * 3, glucose))

coef(fit_ols)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Step 1 — The loss as a function of the parameters

In Exercise 3.2 a loss scored a line someone else supplied. Now treat it as a
function of the two parameters, which is what fitting actually optimises:

$$\text{MSE}(\hat\beta_0, \hat\beta_1) = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{m}
\left( y_i - \left( \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 x_i \right) \right)^2$$

Nothing in that formula is new. The residual, the square and the mean are the
three steps of the last exercise; what has changed is which part you hold fixed.
The data is now the fixed thing and the parameters are what vary.

Start by hand with the first three patients, aged 28, 44 and 26, with glucose
194, 129 and 132. For $\hat\beta_0 = 3$ and $\hat\beta_1 = 5$ the predictions
are 143, 223 and 133, so

$$\frac{(194-143)^2 + (129-223)^2 + (132-133)^2}{3}
 = \frac{2601 + 8836 + 1}{3} = 3812.67$$

Do that arithmetic on paper before you run the cell. The same three steps as
before — predict, subtract, square and average — on the first three rows:

```{r}
glu |>
  slice(1:3) |>
  mutate(pred = 3 + 5 * age,
         r    = glucose - pred) |>
  summarise(MSE = mean(r^2))
```

### Task 1 — Score two candidate lines on all 80 patients

Those two parameter values were picked out of the air. Score them on the whole
dataset, then score a second pair, $\hat\beta_0 = 4$ and $\hat\beta_1 = 7$.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
glu |>
  mutate(r_3_5 = glucose - (3 + 5 * age),
         r_4_7 = glucose - (______)) |>
  summarise(at_3_5 = mean(r_3_5^2),
            at_4_7 = mean(r_4_7^2)) |>
  round(1)
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
glu |>
  mutate(r_3_5 = glucose - (3 + 5 * age),
         r_4_7 = glucose - (4 + 7 * age)) |>
  summarise(at_3_5 = mean(r_3_5^2),
            at_4_7 = mean(r_4_7^2)) |>
  round(1)
```
:::
:::

On all 80 rows those two candidates score 7,462 and 22,991 against the fitted
line's 847.5. Both are terrible, and the first is better than the second, which
is all a loss is for: ranking candidates.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Which number is the intercept
Writing $\hat\beta_0 = 3$, $\hat\beta_1 = 5$ and then drawing
`geom_abline(slope = 3, intercept = 5)` plots a different line from the one you
scored, and the plot will look convincing. `geom_abline()` takes `slope` and
`intercept` by name for exactly this reason. Name both arguments, every time.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Step 2 — Every candidate line at once

Ranking two candidates is a loss doing its job. Fitting is the same idea with
far more candidates. Build a grid of them — 101 intercepts between 60 and 160,
151 slopes between −1 and 2, 15,251 lines in total — pair every candidate with
every patient, and score each candidate under both losses.

```{r}
candidates <- expand_grid(b0 = seq(60, 160, by = 1),
                          b1 = seq(-1, 2, by = 0.02))

scores <- candidates |>
  cross_join(glu |> select(age, glucose)) |>
  mutate(r = glucose - (b0 + b1 * age)) |>
  summarise(MSE = mean(r^2),
            MAE = mean(abs(r)), .by = c(b0, b1))

scores
```

One row per candidate line, with its score under each loss. Draw the MSE
column as a surface, with the line `lm()` returned marked in red.

```{r}
ggplot(scores, aes(x = b0, y = b1)) +
  geom_raster(aes(fill = log10(MSE))) +
  geom_contour(aes(z = log10(MSE)), colour = "white",
               alpha = 0.4, bins = 12) +
  annotate("point", x = coef(fit_ols)[[1]], y = coef(fit_ols)[[2]],
           colour = "red", size = 3) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma") +
  labs(x = expression(hat(beta)[0]), y = expression(hat(beta)[1]),
       fill = "log10(MSE)")
```

That picture is the loss function itself, with one colour for every line you
could have drawn. Two features of it matter for the next exercise. The surface
is a bowl: it has one lowest point and no others, which is why least squares has
a single answer. And the bowl is a long diagonal trough rather than a round
basin, because the intercept and the slope trade off against each other — raise
the slope and you can compensate by lowering the intercept. Exercise 3.4 walks
downhill on this exact surface, and the shape of the trough is what makes that
harder than it sounds.

### Task 2 — Find the best candidate under each loss

Pull the lowest-scoring row out of the grid, first by MSE and then by MAE.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
scores |> slice_min(______, n = 1)
scores |> slice_min(MAE, n = 1)

coef(fit_ols)   # the fitted line, to compare
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
scores |> slice_min(MSE, n = 1)
scores |> slice_min(MAE, n = 1)

coef(fit_ols)   # the fitted line, to compare
```
:::
:::

The best candidate under MSE is intercept 110, slope 0.30, scoring 847.55 —
against `lm()`'s 110.298, 0.2887 and 847.52. The difference is the spacing of
the grid and nothing else. Under MAE the best candidate is a different line:
intercept 99, slope 0.50.

Now do the same on the contaminated data, and watch which of the two losses
changes its mind.

```{r}
scores_bad <- candidates |>
  cross_join(glu_bad |> select(age, glucose)) |>
  mutate(r = glucose - (b0 + b1 * age)) |>
  summarise(MSE = mean(r^2),
            MAE = mean(abs(r)), .by = c(b0, b1))

bind_rows(
  clean_MSE        = scores     |> slice_min(MSE, n = 1) |> select(b0, b1),
  contaminated_MSE = scores_bad |> slice_min(MSE, n = 1) |> select(b0, b1),
  clean_MAE        = scores     |> slice_min(MAE, n = 1) |> select(b0, b1),
  contaminated_MAE = scores_bad |> slice_min(MAE, n = 1) |> select(b0, b1),
  .id = "best_under")
```

| best candidate | intercept | slope |
|---|---|---|
| clean data, by MSE | 110 | **+0.30** |
| contaminated data, by MSE | 136 | **−0.16** |
| clean data, by MAE | 99 | **+0.50** |
| contaminated data, by MAE | 103 | **+0.40** |

: {tbl-colwidths="[46,27,27]"}

Squared error reverses the sign of the slope. Absolute error, given the same
three corrupted patients, still says glucose rises with age. Same data, same
grid of candidates, same arithmetic — only the loss is different.

::: {.callout-note}
## Why not just use the grid
Fifteen thousand evaluations to recover two numbers already feels wasteful, and
it is: the grid also has to be centred near the answer to find it, which
requires knowing the answer. With ten parameters rather than two, a grid of this
resolution would need more evaluations than there are atoms in the room. Grid
search is a teaching device here, not a method.
:::

### Where we left off

Exercise 3.2 scored lines that somebody else had drawn. Load the same 80
patients, fit the line `lm()` chooses, and rebuild the contaminated copy — the
one with patients 1, 3 and 5 tripled — because the last task needs both.

```{python}
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

glu = pd.read_csv("data/glucose_study.csv")

fit_ols = LinearRegression().fit(glu[["age"]], glu["glucose"])

glu_bad = glu.copy()
glu_bad.loc[[0, 2, 4], "glucose"] *= 3

fit_ols.intercept_, fit_ols.coef_[0]
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Step 1 — The loss as a function of the parameters

In Exercise 3.2 a loss scored a line someone else supplied. Now treat it as a
function of the two parameters, which is what fitting actually optimises:

$$\text{MSE}(\hat\beta_0, \hat\beta_1) = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{m}
\left( y_i - \left( \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 x_i \right) \right)^2$$

Nothing in that formula is new. The residual, the square and the mean are the
three steps of the last exercise; what has changed is which part you hold fixed.
The data is now the fixed thing and the parameters are what vary.

Start by hand with the first three patients, aged 28, 44 and 26, with glucose
194, 129 and 132. For $\hat\beta_0 = 3$ and $\hat\beta_1 = 5$ the predictions
are 143, 223 and 133, so

$$\frac{(194-143)^2 + (129-223)^2 + (132-133)^2}{3}
 = \frac{2601 + 8836 + 1}{3} = 3812.67$$

Do that arithmetic on paper before you run the cell. The same three steps as
before — predict, subtract, square and average — on the first three rows:

```{python}
first3 = glu.head(3).copy()
first3["pred"] = 3 + 5 * first3["age"]
first3["r"]    = first3["glucose"] - first3["pred"]

(first3["r"] ** 2).mean()
```

### Task 1 — Score two candidate lines on all 80 patients

Those two parameter values were picked out of the air. Score them on the whole
dataset, then score a second pair, $\hat\beta_0 = 4$ and $\hat\beta_1 = 7$.

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
r_3_5 = glu["glucose"] - (3 + 5 * glu["age"])
r_4_7 = glu["glucose"] - (______)

pd.Series({"at_3_5": (r_3_5 ** 2).mean(),
           "at_4_7": (r_4_7 ** 2).mean()}).round(1)
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
r_3_5 = glu["glucose"] - (3 + 5 * glu["age"])
r_4_7 = glu["glucose"] - (4 + 7 * glu["age"])

pd.Series({"at_3_5": (r_3_5 ** 2).mean(),
           "at_4_7": (r_4_7 ** 2).mean()}).round(1)
```
:::
:::

On all 80 rows those two candidates score 7,462 and 22,991 against the fitted
line's 847.5. Both are terrible, and the first is better than the second, which
is all a loss is for: ranking candidates.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Step 2 — Every candidate line at once

Ranking two candidates is a loss doing its job. Fitting is the same idea with
far more candidates. Build a grid of them — 101 intercepts between 60 and 160,
151 slopes between −1 and 2, 15,251 lines in total — pair every candidate with
every patient, and score each candidate under both losses.

```{python}
b0s = np.arange(60, 161, 1)
b1s = np.round(np.arange(-1, 2.001, 0.02), 2)

candidates = pd.MultiIndex.from_product(
    [b0s, b1s], names=["b0", "b1"]).to_frame(index=False)

scores = candidates.merge(glu[["age", "glucose"]], how="cross")
scores["r"] = scores["glucose"] - (scores["b0"] + scores["b1"] * scores["age"])
scores = (scores.assign(sq=lambda d: d["r"] ** 2,
                        ab=lambda d: d["r"].abs())
                .groupby(["b0", "b1"], as_index=False)
                .agg(MSE=("sq", "mean"), MAE=("ab", "mean")))

scores.head()
```

One row per candidate line, with its score under each loss. Draw the MSE
column as a surface, with the line `lm()` returned marked in red.

(The red point is what `LinearRegression` returned.)

```{python}
surface = scores.pivot(index="b1", columns="b0", values="MSE")

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
cs = ax.contourf(surface.columns, surface.index,
                 np.log10(surface.values), levels=20, cmap="magma")
ax.scatter([fit_ols.intercept_], [fit_ols.coef_[0]], color="red", zorder=3)
cbar = fig.colorbar(cs, ax=ax, label="log10(MSE)")
ax.set_xlabel(r"$\hat\beta_0$")
ax.set_ylabel(r"$\hat\beta_1$")
plt.show()
```

That picture is the loss function itself, with one colour for every line you
could have drawn. Two features of it matter for the next exercise. The surface
is a bowl: it has one lowest point and no others, which is why least squares has
a single answer. And the bowl is a long diagonal trough rather than a round
basin, because the intercept and the slope trade off against each other — raise
the slope and you can compensate by lowering the intercept. Exercise 3.4 walks
downhill on this exact surface, and the shape of the trough is what makes that
harder than it sounds.

### Task 2 — Find the best candidate under each loss

Pull the lowest-scoring row out of the grid, first by MSE and then by MAE.

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
print(scores.nsmallest(1, ______))
print(scores.nsmallest(1, "MAE"))

print(fit_ols.intercept_, fit_ols.coef_[0])   # the fitted line, to compare
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
print(scores.nsmallest(1, "MSE"))
print(scores.nsmallest(1, "MAE"))

print(fit_ols.intercept_, fit_ols.coef_[0])   # the fitted line, to compare
```
:::
:::

The best candidate under MSE is intercept 110, slope 0.30, scoring 847.55 —
against `lm()`'s 110.298, 0.2887 and 847.52. The difference is the spacing of
the grid and nothing else. Under MAE the best candidate is a different line:
intercept 99, slope 0.50.

Now do the same on the contaminated data, and watch which of the two losses
changes its mind.

Read "`lm()`" above as `LinearRegression`: the comparison is the same.

```{python}
scores_bad = candidates.merge(glu_bad[["age", "glucose"]], how="cross")
scores_bad["r"] = (scores_bad["glucose"]
                   - (scores_bad["b0"] + scores_bad["b1"] * scores_bad["age"]))
scores_bad = (scores_bad.assign(sq=lambda d: d["r"] ** 2,
                                ab=lambda d: d["r"].abs())
                        .groupby(["b0", "b1"], as_index=False)
                        .agg(MSE=("sq", "mean"), MAE=("ab", "mean")))

pd.DataFrame(
    [scores.nsmallest(1, "MSE")[["b0", "b1"]].iloc[0],
     scores_bad.nsmallest(1, "MSE")[["b0", "b1"]].iloc[0],
     scores.nsmallest(1, "MAE")[["b0", "b1"]].iloc[0],
     scores_bad.nsmallest(1, "MAE")[["b0", "b1"]].iloc[0]],
    index=["clean_MSE", "contaminated_MSE", "clean_MAE", "contaminated_MAE"])
```

| best candidate | intercept | slope |
|---|---|---|
| clean data, by MSE | 110 | **+0.30** |
| contaminated data, by MSE | 136 | **−0.16** |
| clean data, by MAE | 99 | **+0.50** |
| contaminated data, by MAE | 103 | **+0.40** |

: {tbl-colwidths="[46,27,27]"}

Squared error reverses the sign of the slope. Absolute error, given the same
three corrupted patients, still says glucose rises with age. Same data, same
grid of candidates, same arithmetic — only the loss is different.

::: {.callout-note}
## Why not just use the grid
Fifteen thousand evaluations to recover two numbers already feels wasteful, and
it is: the grid also has to be centred near the answer to find it, which
requires knowing the answer. With ten parameters rather than two, a grid of this
resolution would need more evaluations than there are atoms in the room. Grid
search is a teaching device here, not a method.
:::

::::::

## Reflection

1. The grid's best candidate under squared error is an intercept of 110 and a
   slope of 0.30; `lm()` returns 110.298 and 0.2887. Is the grid wrong?
2. You double the resolution of the grid in both parameters. How many candidate
   lines is that, and how many would the same resolution cost for a model with
   ten parameters rather than two?

::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::: {.instructor}
**Answers.** Reflection 1: no. The grid can only return a point it contains, and
its intercepts are spaced one apart and its slopes 0.02 apart, so 110 and 0.30
are `lm()`'s answer rounded to the grid. The MSE values say the same thing:
847.55 against 847.52, a difference in the third decimal of a quantity measured
in mg/dL squared. Reflection 2: doubling the resolution gives 201 × 301 = 60,501
candidates, four times as many for one more decimal place. The same resolution
in ten parameters is $101^{10}$, which is about $10^{20}$ — this is the part
students should leave with, because it is the reason Exercise 3.4 exists.

**Expected values** (regenerated data varies in the last digit). By hand on the
first three patients, $\hat\beta_0 = 3$, $\hat\beta_1 = 5$: MSE = 3812.67. On
all 80 patients: 7,462.5 at (3, 5) and 22,990.6 at (4, 7), against 847.5 for
the fitted line. Grid: 15,251 candidates; best under MSE is 110 and 0.30 on the
clean data, 136 and −0.16 on the contaminated; best under MAE is 99 and 0.50 on
the clean data, 103 and 0.40 on the contaminated.

**Common failures.** (1) Reading the grid's intercept of 110 as a more accurate
answer than `lm()`'s 110.298; it is the same answer, rounded to the spacing of
the grid. (2) Passing the intercept where `geom_abline()` expects the slope,
which draws a plausible-looking line that is not the one they scored. (3)
Expecting the surface plot to show a round basin, then reading the diagonal
trough as a mistake in the code rather than as the correlation between the two
parameters.

**Plenary.** Put the four-row table up at the end: squared error reverses the
sign of the slope under contamination and absolute error does not. That
reversal is the moment the day's argument lands. Then ask what they would have
done without the grid — the answer is the next exercise.

**Timing.** Each grid pairs 15,251 candidates with 80 patients, which is 1.2
million rows, so expect a pause of a second or two rather than an instant
answer. If you are short, show the surface plot and discuss it rather than
having everyone build the grid; the plot is the part they remember.
:::
:::

## Stretch

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Stretch 1 — Narrow the grid
Take the best candidate you found, build a second grid of 101 intercepts and
151 slopes centred on it but ten times finer, and score that. Compare the answer
with `lm()`'s to three decimal places. Then say how many rounds of this you
would need to match `lm()` exactly, and what that tells you about the method.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Stretch 2 — A loss that is neither
Huber loss is squared for residuals smaller than some cut-off and absolute for
the larger ones. Add a third score to the grid for a cut-off you choose, find
its best candidate on the contaminated data, and then find the cut-off at which
the best slope flips back to positive. That number is the amount of
contamination you have implicitly assumed.
:::

## What you can and cannot now claim

**Can:** that you can write a loss as a function of a model's parameters, score
any candidate pair against the data, and show that fitting is the search for the
lowest point of the surface those scores trace out.

**Cannot:** that you can find that lowest point for any model worth fitting. A
grid of 15,251 candidates recovered two parameters to the spacing of the grid,
and it only worked because the grid was drawn around the answer. Exercise 3.4
replaces the grid with a method that uses the slope of the loss itself.
